tier_reason: The README benchmark table (single core AVX2, Ryzen 5 3600, 1024-byte shards) gives only absolute throughput for this crate; the 'fastest in all cases' statement covers Rust crates run by examples/quick-comparison.rs and publishes no numbers, and no C or C++ (Leopard-RS, ISA-L) figure exists anywhere opened, so there is no measured win over a C/C++ baseline.

corrections.baseline: catid/leopard (C++) and Intel ISA-L (C) named by the lead but never compared; examples/quick-comparison.rs times reed-solomon-16, reed-solomon-erasure (built with the simd-accel feature, whose GF(2^8) multiply kernel is C SIMD code copied from NicolasT/reedsolomon and compiled through cc), reed-solomon-novelpoly and leopard-codec, but the README publishes no numbers for that run
corrections.stars_or_usage: 100 stars, 23 forks; crates.io 3.1.0, about 2.19M downloads (about 432k recent)
corrections.caveats: Lead asked for a comparison with catid/leopard (C++) or ISA-L; none in the README, CHANGELOG or examples/quick-comparison.rs. catid/leopard's Benchmarks.md gives MB/s on an unstated 'few year old laptop' with 64 KB pieces, 128:128 Input=1964.98 MB/s encode, which cannot be compared with this crate's 1024-byte-shard Ryzen figures (different shard size, hardware and byte accounting; 'not very rigorous' by its author), so no ratio is derived. The 'fastest' claim is first-party, covers Rust crates only and has no published numbers; the closest thing to a C baseline in it is reed-solomon-erasure with simd-accel (C SIMD GF(2^8) multiply inside a Rust O(n*k) matrix codec, a different algorithm from this crate's O(n log n) GF(2^16) FFT), so even a run of it would not be a like-for-like language comparison. README says the crate is a fork of Markus Laire's reed-solomon-16 crate, itself based on Leopard-RS (BSD-3-Clause code carried in the LICENSE); not a GitHub fork. One-time table initialisation under 10 ms can dominate tiny inputs; decoding with about 42 or fewer recovery shards is not the fastest even among the Rust crates. A web search found no head-to-head with Leopard C++ or ISA-L. Not a language-level claim: the speed comes from the FFT-based Leopard algorithm plus runtime-selected AVX2/SSSE3/Neon kernels.

notes: Real, widely used crate (about 2.19M crates.io downloads) but no measured C/C++ comparison; keep at D with shortcoming 'no C or C++ baseline measured; fastest claim covers Rust crates only, unpublished'. Metadata checked: MIT AND BSD-3-Clause (Cargo.toml and LICENSE), last commit 2025-10-14 (v3.1.0), active.

tier_reason: The numbers come from the author's own executed notebook vis/block_aligner_bench_vis.ipynb (benchmark code in examples/nanopore_bench_global.rs, uc_bench, pssm_bench), with no CPU model and unstated C/C++ build flags, so first-party with partial methodology; the peer-reviewed Bioinformatics 2023 paper that could justify B was unreachable (doi, OUP, PMC, bioRxiv blocked) and is known here only from a search snippet ('5-10x faster than some previous methods'), which the wave rule caps at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Saved notebook outputs in vis/block_aligner_bench_vis.ipynb, total seconds, 'ours (1%-1%)' with traceback vs baselines: Illumina 0.331 s vs Edlib 1.078, ksw_extz2_sse(1%) 0.702, ksw_extz2_sse(10%) 0.662, parasail 1.877, WFA2 0.0396, WFA2 adaptive 0.0338; Nanopore 1kbp 0.355 vs Edlib 0.982, ksw2(1%) 0.690, ksw2(10%) 1.492, WFA2 1.074, WFA2 adaptive 0.968, parasail 4.241; Nanopore under 10kbp 1.233 vs Edlib 4.182, ksw2(1%) 2.041, ksw2(10%) 13.948, WFA2 12.232, WFA2 adaptive 2.636, parasail 35.789; Nanopore under 50kbp 29.619 vs Edlib 63.197, ksw2(1%) 44.493, ksw2(10%) 571.018, WFA2 331.475, WFA2 adaptive 58.830 (parasail not run). Derived from page data: block-aligner is 2.1x to 3.4x faster than Edlib, 1.5x to 2.1x faster than banded ksw2 at 1% band, 5.7x to 29x faster than parasail, but about 8.4x SLOWER than exact WFA2 on Illumina reads. Protein Uniclust30 (no traceback, block 32-256) 0.0886 s vs parasail 0.8250 s (9.3x, derived); with traceback 0.1698 s (4.9x, derived). SCOP profile pairs 0.149 s (block 32-32) vs parasail 0.597 s (4.0x, derived). The same notebook's 25 kbp Nanopore benchmark shows block-aligner SLOWER than the C aligners from diff-bench-paper: ours (no trace 32-32) 0.991 s and (trace 32-32) 1.378 s against libgaba 0.433 s, Suzuki-Kasahara editdist 0.480 s, diff-raw 0.611 s and non-diff 0.676 s fill time, while Edlib took 28.0 s and SeqAn 90.3 s (about 2.3x slower than libgaba, derived from page data; the C rows come from a separate harness, custom_bench.sh, and count fill time only).
corrections.caveats: The Bioinformatics paper (Liu and Steinegger 2023, btad487) could not be opened (doi, academic.oup.com, PMC and bioRxiv are blocked here), so the numbers come from the repo's executed benchmark notebook, which the README says reproduces the manuscript experiments; a search-result snippet of the paper abstract says 5-10x faster than some previous methods with under 3% error on protein and long-read data (snippet only). Not like-for-like: block-aligner is an approximate aligner while Edlib (unit-cost edit distance), parasail and WFA2 without heuristic are exact and use different scoring models, and ksw2 is banded; in examples/nanopore_bench_global.rs parasail is called through global_alignment_score (score only, no traceback) while block-aligner, Edlib (EDLIB_TASK_PATH), WFA2 (AlignmentScope::Alignment) and ksw_extz2_sse (score-only flag left at 0) compute a path, which favours parasail; the speedup over parasail grows with length because parasail does full O(nm) DP. WFA2 is far faster than block-aligner on low-error short reads, and on the notebook's 25 kbp Nanopore set the C aligners libgaba and the Suzuki-Kasahara difference-recurrence codes from diff-bench-paper beat it by about 2x (cross-harness, fill time only). The C/C++ baselines are reached through forked binding crates (parasailors, edlib_rs with logging removed, rust-wfa2 fork with 'small changes that ensures wfa2 code autovectorizes', ksw2-sys), so call overhead and build flags may differ from stock builds. Single saved run, no error bars, no CPU model; datasets must be downloaded separately (data/README.md). Lead came from the A*PA2 enricher (pa-bench lists block-aligner as an approximate aligner); the pa-bench result files were not reachable. Not a language-level claim: the win is algorithmic (adaptive approximate blocks), not Rust codegen.

notes: Downgrade B to C: tier B rested on a paper nobody could open; the repo notebook is first-party, no CPU model, C/C++ flags unstated. Shortcomings: approximate vs exact aligners, parasail score-only, 8.4x slower than WFA2 on Illumina and about 2x slower than libgaba on 25 kbp Nanopore; stale (last commit 2024-06-23). Candidate for a paper-access retier to B if the Bioinformatics paper's per-tool figures are reached.
